summary: Specifies how to carry IPv6, IPv4, and ARP packets over Fibre Channel. It also describes how to form IPv6 link-local and autoconfigured addresses on Fibre Channel and how to resolve IPv4 addresses there. It obsoletes RFC 2625 and RFC 3831, and was later updated by RFC 5494 and RFC 8064.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC specifies how IPv4, IPv6, and ARP packets are carried over Fibre Channel. It also explains how ports form IPv6 addresses and find the Fibre Channel addresses needed to send packets.

questions: how does ip work over fibre channel
what is the default mtu for ip over fibre channel
subtitle: How Fibre Channel carries IPv4, IPv6, and ARP traffic between ports.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel networks need rules for carrying IP traffic and resolving addresses, including for devices with different Fibre Channel name formats.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC wraps each IP or ARP packet in a Fibre Channel Network_Header and LLC/SNAP header, then carries it in Fibre Channel frames. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery; IPv4 uses a Fibre Channel-specific ARP format.
tldr.outcome: It combines IPv4, IPv6, and ARP operation in one specification, obsoletes RFC 2625 and RFC 3831, and is updated by RFC 5494 and RFC 8064.

today: RFC 4338 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2625 and RFC 3831. It is updated by RFC 5494 and RFC 8064.

sections.title: Why One IP-over-Fibre-Channel Specification
sections.content:
Earlier RFCs described IPv4 and IPv6 over Fibre Channel separately. RFC 4338 combines those rules and broadens IPv4 support to Fibre Channel devices with name formats beyond format 0x1.

It also defines IPv4 multicast transmission and a Fibre Channel-specific ARP format, replacing the older requirement to use FARP for address resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC combines the earlier IPv4 and IPv6 rules for Fibre Channel. It also supports more device-name formats and defines how IPv4 multicast and address lookup work.

sections.title: Ports, Names, and Addresses
sections.content:
A Fibre Channel network connects nodes through ports. An Nx_Port has a permanent 64-bit N_Port_Name and a temporary 24-bit N_Port_ID. The name identifies the port, while the ID is used to route Fibre Channel frames.

A port obtains its N_Port_ID through Fabric Login, and two ports complete Port Login before communicating effectively. Because the ID can change after some link events, a port must validate the name-to-ID mapping before relying on it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each port has a stable name and a temporary routing ID. The stable name identifies the port; the current ID tells Fibre Channel where to deliver frames.

sections.title: Wrapping IP and ARP Packets
sections.content:
An IP or ARP Information Unit MUST include a 16-octet Fibre Channel Network_Header and an 8-octet LLC/SNAP header. In a multi-frame IP sequence, only the first frame carries these headers; later frames carry the remaining packet data.

The LLC/SNAP PID identifies IPv6 as 0x86DD, IPv4 as 0x0800, or ARP as 0x0806. Class 3 service is required for multicast and control traffic and recommended for other unicast IP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is preceded by two headers: one carries the Fibre Channel port names, and the other identifies the packet type. A long packet uses multiple frames, with these headers on the first frame.

sections.title: Maximum Transfer Unit
sections.content:
The default MTU for IPv4 and IPv6 packets over Fibre Channel is 65280 octets. It can be reduced by configuration, and IPv6 Router Advertisements can specify a smaller value. IPv6's MTU MUST NOT be lower than 1280 octets.

To support that minimum IPv6 MTU with the Fibre Channel headers, an Nx_Port must handle an Information Unit of at least 1304 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Fibre Channel has a default IP packet MTU of 65280 octets, but the configured value can be smaller. IPv6 still requires an MTU of at least 1280 octets, plus space for the Fibre Channel headers.

sections.title: Forming IPv6 Addresses
sections.content:
An Nx_Port derives its IPv6 Interface Identifier from an EUI-64 address based on its N_Port_Name. The conversion complements the Universal/Local bit. Stateless address autoconfiguration uses a 64-bit IPv6 prefix.

The link-local address is formed by appending the Interface Identifier to FE80::/64. The RFC describes conversions for name formats 0x1, 0x2, 0x5, and EUI-64-mapped formats 0xC through 0xF.
sections.plainLanguage: A Fibre Channel port can derive its IPv6 interface identifier from its permanent N_Port_Name. The link-local address combines that identifier with the specified link-local prefix.

sections.title: Resolving IPv4 and IPv6 Destinations
sections.content:
Both the N_Port_Name and N_Port_ID are needed to send a unicast packet to another port. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery, with a link-layer address containing the port name and ID.

IPv4 uses Fibre Channel ARP, a 40-octet packet that carries both identifiers. If the sender has no valid mapping and Port Login, it broadcasts an ARP request. The port with the matching IPv4 address records the sender's mapping and replies directly.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery to learn a destination port's Fibre Channel address. IPv4 uses a Fibre Channel ARP request, and the matching port replies with its name and current routing ID.

sections.title: Compatibility, Security, and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC expects IPv4 packet transmission to interoperate with RFC 2625. Its address-resolution method differs, and a port with a format 0x1 name can use an administratively configurable compatibility mode that sends both Fibre Channel and Ethernet ARP requests.

The RFC says IP and ARP add no security concerns beyond Fibre Channel. Soft zoning based on FC Name Server masking does not work for IP traffic because IPv4 and IPv6 do not use that name server. Fibre Channel ESP or IP-layer security techniques may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Compatibility mode supports communication with older RFC 2625 implementations. IP traffic does not use Fibre Channel Name Server masking, but Fibre Channel ESP and IP-layer security can protect it.
